Program in Computer and Statistical Sciences The Ph.D. will have 2 different concentrations: Computer Science, and Statistics.
Some of the prerequisites are common, other are concentration specific.
Ph.D.
Program Prerequisites Admission to this program requires a Bachelors degree in Computer Science, Statistics, Biostatistics, Mathematics, Engineering, or a closely related field.
A Master’s degree is encouraged but not required.
Common requirements include course work covering the material in the following courses: • MTH 141 – Calculus 1 • MTH 142 – Calculus 2 • MTH 215 – Introduction to Linear Algebra • One course in Mathematics or Statistics for which calculus is a prerequisite All applicants will need to take the GRE.
In addition, international applicants will need to report their TOEFL scores.
Waivers can be granted at the discretion of the graduate director.
GRE subject in Mathematics or Computer Science are not required but can be favorably assessed by the admission committee.

Specific Prerequisites for Computer Science Concentration In addition to the general requirements applicants with a bachelors degree in an unrelated field will be considered provided they have completed course work covering the material in • CSC 211 Object-Oriented Programming • CSC 212 Data Structures and Abstractions • CSC 301 Fundamentals of Programming Languages • CSC 340: Applied Combinatorics • CSC 440 Design and Analysis of Algorithms Specific Prerequisites for Statistics Concentration In addition to the general requirements, following courses or their equivalents (will need approval of the graduate program chair) may be required to be admitted to our program if a student lacks a strong quantitative background.
However, these requirements may be waived based on prior experience in industry or research.

• MTH 243 – Calculus for Functions of Several Variables • STA 409 – Statistical Methods in Research I • STA 412 – Statistical Methods in Research II • MTH 451 – Intro Probability and Statistics • MTH 452 - Mathematical Statistics Ph.D.
Program Requirements The student must complete a total of at least 72 academic credits beyond the bachelors degree as follows: • At least 52 credits in coursework or 14 classes (3 or 4 credits each) • At least 18 dissertation research credits • At least 2 credit hours in seminar series (1 credit hour per semester).
Attendance strongly encouraged for all full time students.
A student entering the program with an M.S. degree in Computer Science, Statistics or a related area may be granted up to 30 credits toward the Ph.D. in Computer and Statistical Sciences.
A program of study can include at most three courses at the 400-level.
Students who have undergraduate credits for a particular 400-level course (or equivalent) cannot repeat the course for graduate credit.

Specific Requirements for Computer Science Concentration Students must complete: • Four graduate CSC courses decided after consulting the graduate committee. • Four more CSC courses or equivalent approved by the student’s advisor or major professor. • At least one graduate STA course approved by the student’s advisor or major professor. • Other courses must be selected in order to meet the coursework minimum and will be selected in consultation with the student’s advisor or major professor.
Specific Requirements for Statistics Concentration Students must complete: • Five graduate STA courses decided after consulting the graduate committee. • Four more graduate statistics courses approved by the student’s advisor or major professor. • At least one CSC graduate course approved by the student’s advisor or major professor. • Other courses must be selected in order to meet the coursework minimum and will be selected in consultation with the student’s advisor or major professor.

Milestone 1: Qualifying Exam The qualifying examination will consist of written exams, with the purpose of testing the student’s knowledge of specific core areas for their concentration of studies. A waiver could be granted to a student from taking an exam in one of the areas where the student can demonstrate competence in that area. Waivers could be granted at the time of admission. The qualifying examination should be taken within the first 30 program credits. Core areas for Computer Science Concentration Qualifying Exam The qualifying examination requirements cover the material of CSC 301, 340, 411, 412, 440, and 445. These requirements are checked at the time of admission Core areas for Statistics Concentration Qualifying Exam The qualifying examination requirements cover the material of MTH 451 and 452, STA 502, 542, and 545. These requirements are checked at the time of admission. Milestone 2: Comprehensive Exam Students must take a comprehensive examination, which is composed of a written examination and an oral examination. Typically, a student would be expected to take the comprehensive examination within two years after joining the program. A candidate whose comprehensive exam performance is deemed as failing by the Graduate Committee may, with the recommendation of the committee and the approval of the Graduate School, be permitted one re-examination, to be taken no sooner than four months and no later than one year after the initial examination. Milestone 3: Dissertation Defense Students are expected to write a Ph.D. dissertation, under the supervision of a Major Professor and a graduate committee, according to the rules established by the Graduate School.

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) The department of Mathematics and Applied Mathematical Sciences is proposing to add a track in the existing Ph.D.
Mathematics degree.
Currently, there are two tracks, pure mathematics and applied mathematics.
The proposed track, mathematical statistics and probability, does not fit into either current track as it is a unique combination of pure and applied mathematics.
The new track reflects on the recently growing area of applications and theoretical development at the intersection of probability theory and statistics.
This unique blend between pure and applied mathematics, probability theory/applications and

2 mathematical statistics, makes this combination uniquely deserving a track in the Ph.D. program.
The proposed track targets the same audience as the mathematics department at our aspire to-be-like institution1, University of Connecticut, program, Ph.D. in Mathematics with thesis in Actuarial Science2.
Like, University of Connecticut’s track our proposed track is aimed at attracting students for employment in the financial area to work in industry e.g., brokerage, hedge funds, actuarial science, and insurance companies.
However, unlike University of Connecticut, our track needs to be more broad than focused, since many of our students we do attract are seeking employment in academia and almost all academic settings our students get employed are departments of mathematics and statistics.
Furthermore, we are a much smaller mathematics department than University of Connecticut and cannot create a too focused track.
According to the AMS classification of mathematics departments3, URI’s mathematics department is considered a small public math department.
We currently have 14 tenure-track faculty and 9 Ph.D. students.

Despite these small numbers, the faculty are highly productive, graduating 2-3 students on average per year4, but the number of graduate students has declined over the years from a high of 17 Ph.D. students in 2011-2012 to the current level of 9 students4.
This declined negatively impacts research.
This track is a much needed track aimed at attracting new graduate students (in line with URI 2016-2021 Academic Strategic Plan Goals 1 and 2 – see C1 Institutional Role) 5 and to further develop our growing area of probability, financial math, and actuarial science.

Why is the new program being developed?
The new track, mathematical statistics and probability, is filling in a gap in the Ph.D. program as a combination of pure mathematics and applied mathematics with additional benefit of application (applied skills) in areas that are highly desirable for employment (see B2a).
The new track focuses on the research area of the mathematical theory underlying statistical methods and their use; including probability theory, stochastic processes, Markov processes, and Banach spaces.
All of these areas are underlying structures in several new program endeavors at URI, actuarial science and data science.
These programs are not mutually exclusive.
URI cannot develop new programs at a research university without providing a research foundation.
The development of undergraduate degrees needs a strong, relevant foundational graduate programs to attract graduate students and researchers so that all programs can be cutting edge and move forward in this ever-changing modern world of mathematics.

In 2015, the faculty in the department developed a pre-actuarial program in conjunction with the College of Business which followed shortly afterwards with a tenure-track hire in financial mathematics to help foster the growth.
Since 2016, we worked on the development of the data science program and have been participating in research and curricula development and are also participating in the online graduate certificate in Data Science.
In 2018, we were given a position in probability theory to expand our current research program in this area.
Unfortunately, the faculty member resigned in 2020 – however we were reassured by Dean Riley that the position remains in the department and we will be searching in 2021.
By supporting this new track, URI would not only increase its much-needed graduate enrollment in mathematics and generate new revenue, but also establish itself as a provider of researchers in the area mathematical statistics and probability while growing and firmly establishing the building blocks of the actuarial science and data science programs.

In 1929, famous mathematician, Bertrand Russell stated, “Probability is the most important concept in modern science, especially, as nobody has the slightest notion what it means.” The importance of probability is even more true in this modern age with the need to predict and examine data.
We hope to change the notion that nobody understands what it means.
